Recognize when records describe variables occurring together.
State that an observed pattern alone does not establish a causal direction.
Identify a question about changing a treatment and observing an outcome.
Distinguish observing existing values from deliberately setting a value.
Distinguish the partly hidden world, observed data, and a model of how the world may work.
Distinguish a pattern supported by data from a causal assumption.
Use node, arrow, path, and DAG as names for visible causal-model assumptions.
Recognize that a cause can change a probability without determining every individual outcome.

resources.text: A clinic records each patient's resting heart rate. Could resting heart rate be a variable?
A hospital dashboard records the number of ward alerts each hour. Is the alert count a variable?
Ask whether the item could have a different value for another record or time.
A variable is a recorded feature that can take different values across cases or times.
Yes. Different patients or hours can have different values, so this is a variable.
The value is not fixed by the story; it can vary across records, which is what makes it a variable.
Clinic records show that patients reporting more weekly walking also tend to have lower resting heart rates. What can we say about this relationship based on these observations?
A clinic log shows that patients who use its patient portal more often also attend more scheduled appointments. Does the log show an observed association?
Look for two recorded variables that occur together or vary together.
An association is a pattern in records: values of two variables occur or vary together.
Yes. The records describe how two variables vary together; that is an observed association.
The question asks only whether the recorded pattern co-occurs, not whether it has already established a cause.
A clinic records that patients receiving Treatment A recover less often than patients who do not receive it. Do these records alone establish that Treatment A causes poorer recovery?
A synthetic campus log records umbrella carrying and wet pavement. Would giving everyone an umbrella change how often the pavement is wet? Investigate before making that claim.
Ask whether another cause or another causal direction could fit the same observed pattern.
A pattern in records can be associated without telling us the causal direction or mechanism.
Correct choice: the observed pattern alone does not establish a causal direction. This records one classification, not mastery of causal reasoning.
Treating co-occurrence as a causal direction skips the assumptions needed to distinguish causal explanations.

Mission: would making everyone carry an umbrella change how often the pavement is wet? Inspect the campus records, propose a model and prediction, reveal the teaching model's result, then revise your explanation.

Each record is one person's arrival at campus. Pavement wetness describes the pavement at that arrival. These are 240 arrival records, not 240 different days. The records show umbrella carrying and wet pavement together, but do not say why.

Arrows are proposed causes, not facts established by the records. Compare umbrella carrying causing wet pavement, the reverse direction, or rain as a common cause. More than one model can fit these observations.
Imagine the same 240 arrivals, with umbrella carrying deliberately set to yes for everyone. What do you predict would happen to how often the pavement is wet?

Keep all 240 arrival records and the same background conditions. Set umbrella carrying to yes for everyone, including the 144 arrivals originally without an umbrella. This changes carrying; it does not select only the original umbrella carriers. Reveal the prewritten result for this teaching model; it is not calculated from your proposed arrows.

All 240 arrival records remain: 96 wet and 144 dry, so 40% are wet, unchanged from before. Filtering the original records to umbrella carriers would instead retain only 96 records, all wet (100%). Selecting existing carriers and making everyone carry an umbrella are different comparisons. This is the supplied teaching model's result, not a real-world experiment.

Compare your prediction with the unchanged wet-pavement proportion. This one test does not uniquely identify a graph. For the final model-building exercise, use these supplied assumptions: rain causes umbrella carrying and pavement wetness, with no other direct arrows among these three variables. Revise your graph and separate what came from the test from what was supplied.

Making everyone carry an umbrella left pavement wetness unchanged in this teaching model. Filtering the original umbrella carriers would have produced a different proportion. The final graph check asks you to represent the supplied assumptions: rain causes umbrella carrying and wet pavement, with no other direct arrows among these variables. The test alone did not identify a unique graph. Your prediction and reflection are recorded, not scored as correct reasoning.
A clinician asks whether a patient's recovery would change if they were given a different drug dose. Is this a causal question?
A physiotherapy study asks what would happen to mobility if the assigned weekly session schedule were changed. Is this a treatment-and-outcome question?
Identify what is deliberately changed and which result is being asked about.
Treatment-and-outcome reasoning asks about changing one variable and the resulting outcome.
Yes. The question explicitly asks about changing a treatment and the outcome that follows.
The key feature is the proposed change to a treatment and its outcome, not merely a pattern already recorded.
A clinic records its patients' existing sleep durations without assigning a sleep schedule. Is the clinic observing sleep or intervening on it?
A clinical team compares patients who already chose a symptom-tracking app with those who did not. The team does not assign app use. Is this observation or an intervention on app use?
Ask who deliberately set the value, rather than merely recording an existing value.
Observation records existing values. An intervention deliberately sets or changes a value.
Correct. No one assigned the value, so the evidence is observational rather than interventional.
Recording or comparing existing choices is not the same as deliberately setting the value.
An investigator draws a diagram explaining how a hidden illness process might generate observed clinical records. Is the diagram data or a model?
A hospital engineer draws a proposed explanation of how a laboratory device's internal calibration process might produce drifting sensor readings. Is that explanatory drawing data or a model?
Separate the records we can see from an explanation of the partly hidden system.
Data are observed records; a model is an explanation of how the partly hidden world may work.
Correct. The drawing is an explanatory model, not the data themselves.
An explanation of hidden processes is a model; the observed logs or records are the data.

Clinic records show that patients flagged for review also have more symptoms. Is the claim that illness severity causes both the review flag and the symptoms an observation directly supported by these records, or an additional causal assumption?

A clinic log shows that patients who use a symptom tracker more often also contact nurses more often. Is the claim that symptom severity causes both behaviours a direct observation from this log or an additional causal assumption?
Ask whether the statement reports a recorded pattern or adds a causal mechanism to explain it.
Data can support an observed pattern. A causal direction or mechanism is an additional assumption that should be stated.
Correct. The causal explanation goes beyond the observed pattern, so it is an assumption.
The records may support co-occurrence, but they do not directly record the proposed causal explanation.
In a clinician's proposed causal diagram, what does an arrow from drug dose to symptom score represent?
In a proposed diagram relating physiotherapy, mobility and readiness for discharge, what does a connected route through arrows represent: a path or a node?
Recall that nodes name variables, arrows name proposed directions, and connected routes are paths.
A node represents a variable, an arrow a proposed direction, and a path a connected route through arrows in a DAG.
Correct. The named graphical feature makes an assumption visible; it is not an observed numeric value.
Keep the graph terms separate: nodes are variables, arrows are directions, and paths are connected routes.
Suppose a treatment raises the chance of recovery, but some treated patients still do not recover. Is the effect probabilistic or deterministic?
Suppose an exercise programme lowers the chance of readmission, but some patients who receive it are still readmitted. Is the effect probabilistic or deterministic?
Ask whether the cause changes what is likely, or guarantees the same outcome for every individual.
A causal effect can change an outcome probability without determining every individual result.
Correct. The cause changes a probability, not a guaranteed outcome for every individual.
A changed chance is not a guarantee. Individual outcomes can still differ under a probabilistic effect.

A clinical team records that patients with longer voluntary sleep tend to have better concentration and recovery, then draws a DAG to explain the pattern. Which conclusion is justified by these records without adding a causal assumption?
Separate the recorded association from the causal model and from what would happen if sleep were deliberately assigned.
The records establish an association. The DAG is a model with explicit causal assumptions, and an intervention would require deliberately setting sleep rather than only observing it.
Correct choice on this association-versus-causation check. The records do not establish the proposed intervention effect. This single decision does not assess all nine M0 concepts.
That conclusion treats an observed pattern and a model drawing as if they already proved an intervention effect. Those are different kinds of information.

Represent the supplied simulator assumptions, not a graph claimed to be uniquely discovered: rain causes both umbrella carrying and pavement wetness, with no other direct arrows among these three variables.
Your graph matches the supplied simulator assumptions. This is a model-representation check, not proof that the data identified a unique graph. Your prediction and reflection remain unscored.

This graph does not yet represent the supplied simulator assumptions. For this exercise, include rain causing umbrella carrying and wet pavement, with no other direct arrows. Other graphs may fit the observed pattern; this check is not causal discovery.
A clinic records resting heart rates of 64, 72 and 80 beats per minute. Which part names the variable, and which parts are values?
Synthetic clinical records; no real patient data. Expert content review pending.
Resting heart rate is the feature collected for each patient. The variable's name tells us what each reading concerns.
A value of 72 beats per minute is one reading of heart rate. It is not a separate variable called 72.
Other patients or later records can have different readings. The feature stays resting heart rate even when its value changes.
A variable can take different values across cases or times. A particular measurement is a value of that variable.
Repeated identical readings in a small dataset do not, by themselves, mean the clinical feature cannot vary.
Name the feature, the case and the reading before comparing patients.
In clinic records, patients reporting more weekly walking also tend to have lower resting heart rates. What pattern has been recorded?
Synthetic clinical example; not a finding about exercise or heart health. Expert content review pending.
The records include reported walking and resting heart rate. Each patient's row contains a value for each variable.
In this supplied dataset, higher walking values tend to occur with lower heart-rate values. Association can run in opposite directions.
Report that relationship across the recorded cases. A single low heart-rate measurement is not itself the relationship between walking and heart rate.
An observed association is a pattern in how variables occur together or vary together in clinical records.
Do not require both values to increase. A recorded relationship can involve one increasing while the other decreases.
Describe the two variables and the recorded pattern before asking for an explanation.
A clinic records poorer recovery among patients receiving Treatment A. Does that recorded difference establish that Treatment A harms recovery?
Treatment A and these records are hypothetical; possible mechanisms are hypotheses. Expert content review pending.
Treatment receipt and recovery differ across the recorded groups. This describes an association, not the outcome of assigning different treatments to comparable patients.
Patients with more severe illness might be more likely to receive Treatment A and less likely to recover. This is a hypothesis about the records, not an established explanation.
The group difference alone does not establish harm, benefit or no effect. A possible severity difference does not settle the treatment's effect either.
Only proposed common-cause paths are shown. This partial hypothesis does not assert that severity explains everything or that Treatment A has no effect.
Association describes how variables vary together. A recorded association alone does not establish a causal direction or a treatment effect.
Poorer recovery in a treated group is not, by itself, proof of harm. A plausible alternative explanation is not proof of benefit or no effect.
Separate the observed group difference, a proposed explanation and the effect of assigning treatment.
A clinician asks what would happen to recovery if a drug dose were changed. What is being changed, and what result is being asked about?
Synthetic question about a treatment; no benefit or dose recommendation. Expert content review pending.
The proposed change concerns drug dose. Here treatment names the intervention whose consequence the question asks about.
Recovery is the result of interest. A clear outcome tells the reader which consequence of the proposed change matters.
What would happen to recovery if the dose changed? This is a treatment-and-outcome question even though no direction or size of effect has been established.
A treatment-and-outcome question asks what would happen to an outcome if a treatment were changed.
A well-framed clinical question does not prove that the proposed treatment helps or harms.
State the proposed treatment change and name the outcome you want to understand.
A clinic reads patients' existing sleep durations from their records. Did the clinic assign those durations by recording them?
Synthetic records; no real sleep intervention or health effect. Expert content review pending.
The clinic records sleep that already occurred. No assigned sleep duration is described in this example.
A separate study might deliberately assign a schedule. That changes how a value is set instead of merely reading an existing value.
Comparing existing long-sleep and short-sleep groups still records their existing values. Grouping patients does not itself assign their sleep.
Observation records existing values. An intervention deliberately sets or changes a variable, replacing how that value would otherwise arise.
Selecting patients who already chose an app or behaviour is different from assigning that choice.
Ask how the value arose: was it recorded as it was, or deliberately set?
An investigator has laboratory readings and a drawing of how a hidden illness process might produce them. Which object is the explanatory model?
Synthetic measurements and hypothetical illness model; no verified disease mechanism. Expert content review pending.
The patient's system produces what can be measured. The investigator may not observe every process operating within it.
The recorded laboratory readings are observations. They are not a complete account of every hidden process.
The drawing offers an explanation of how the partly hidden system might work. It is a model, rather than another measured laboratory reading.
The world is the partly hidden system, data are observed records, and a model is an explanation of how that system may work.
Do not treat the labels and arrows in an explanatory drawing as if they were additional measurements.
Keep patient process, observed record and explanatory model distinct.
Records show that patients who contact a nurse more often also report more symptoms. Is saying illness severity causes both just another description of those records?
Synthetic clinical pattern and proposed explanation; not a finding about nursing or illness. Expert content review pending.
The supplied records contain values for nurse contact and reported symptoms. The example says those variables vary together.
Saying severity causes both variables proposes how the pattern might be produced. It adds a mechanism rather than repeating the observed relationship.
Write that severity is a proposed shared explanation. It remains an assumption in this example, not a causal mechanism directly established by the records.
Clinical data can support a pattern. A causal direction or mechanism is an additional assumption that should be stated explicitly.
Clinical plausibility and familiarity do not make a proposed explanation a directly observed fact.
Separate what was recorded from what the clinical causal model assumes.
Recall the shared umbrella investigation. Its three-variable picture is a useful starting point for reading clinical diagrams: first name variables, then proposed causal directions.
Synthetic proposed clinical diagram; no true drug mechanism or effect is asserted. Expert content review pending.
Rain, umbrella carrying and pavement wetness are the three nodes. A clinical diagram uses the same convention: a node could name dose or symptom score, rather than one patient's particular reading.

The two rain arrows express the simulator's supplied model. Likewise, a dose → symptom arrow in a clinical hypothesis states a causal direction; the drawing itself is not a clinical result or an effect size.

Umbrella carrying ← Rain → pavement wetness is a connected path through a common cause, not a directed path from carrying umbrellas to wetness. A DAG has arrows but no directed cycle; following arrow directions cannot return to the starting node.
These are the teaching simulator's assumptions. The unchanged intervention result did not, on its own, prove this unique graph. Clinical graphs require their own justified assumptions.
Nodes represent variables, arrows represent proposed directions, and paths are connected routes through arrows in a DAG.
An arrow in a clinical hypothesis is not a numerical result or proof that the proposed relation is true.
Identify the node, arrow or path, then say which modelling assumption it displays.
Suppose giving Treatment T increases the chance of recovery, but some treated patients still do not recover. Can both statements be true?
Hypothetical treatment example; not a clinical finding or recommendation.
The example says that recovery is more likely with Treatment T than without it.
More likely does not mean certain. Some treated patients may still not recover.
A treatment can change the chance of recovery without guaranteeing recovery for every patient.
A cause can change an outcome's probability without determining every individual outcome.
One patient not recovering does not contradict a higher chance of recovery. This hypothetical example does not establish a real treatment benefit.
Separate a better chance from a guaranteed result.

The deliberate assignment is the intervention. Random assignment does not guarantee a beneficial effect or an identical outcome for everyone.

A proposed mechanism belongs to the model. It may concern an unmeasured part of the world, but proposing it does not make it observed data or establish that it is true.

A claim about what causes attendance and scores is an additional causal assumption. Row counts, recorded means and recorded columns describe the data.

A claim about what causes attendance and scores is an additional causal assumption. Row counts, recorded means and recorded columns describe the data.
